propositions.text: The Principal and Associate Appellants are Bangladeshi citizens appealing an RPD decision denying refugee status.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX (the Associate Appellant) are citizens of Bangladesh. They have appealed a denial of a Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision that found that they are not Convention refugees and/or persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal and Associate Appellants are Bangladeshi citizens appealing an RPD decision denying refugee status.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed; the RPD was correct that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection due to an internal flight alternative.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. I do so, as I find that there is an internal flight alternative for the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The appeal is dismissed; the RPD was correct that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection due to an internal flight alternative.

propositions.text: The Appellants base their claims on the following facts.
propositions.quote: The Appellants base their claims on the following.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants base their claims on the following facts.

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant owned a business in Dhaka for about 10 years and began having problems with Islamic militants in 2017.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant owned a business in Dhaka, Bangladesh, that XXXX XXXX XXXX from Malaysia. He owned this business for about 10 years. He travelled for work, and when he did so, his wife went into the office. In 2017, he began to have problems with Islamic militants.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Appellant owned a business in Dhaka for about 10 years and began having problems with Islamic militants in 2017.

propositions.text: In 2017 and 2018, ABT militants tried to recruit the Principal Appellant, threatened him and his wife, locked them in the office, and took a key.
propositions.quote: On two occasions in XXXX 2017, members of the Ansulrullah Bangla Team (ABT) went to his business and tried to recruit him. They demanded money. He could not pay them but asked for time to do so; in XXXX 2018, they came back. They locked the Principal Appellant and the employees in the office. They brandished weapons at them. Again, they threatened the Principal Appellant and his wife. They took a key when they left the office.

paragraphs.summary: In 2017 and 2018, ABT militants tried to recruit the Principal Appellant, threatened him and his wife, locked them in the office, and took a key.

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant left Dhaka to live with his mother in a village outside Dhaka from about XXXX XXXX to XXXX XXXX 2018.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant left Dhaka. He went to live with his mother in a village outside of Dhaka. He stayed there from around XXXX XXXX to XXXX XXXX, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Appellant left Dhaka to live with his mother in a village outside Dhaka from about XXXX XXXX to XXXX XXXX 2018.

propositions.text: While with his mother, the Principal Appellant received threatening calls; ABT came to her house but he was absent; he then stayed with a friend in Dhaka and still received calls.
propositions.quote: While he was with his mother, he received threatening phone calls. The ABT went to her house, but he was not there. He left to stay with a friend back in Dhaka. He still received phone calls.

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant left Bangladesh in XXXX 2018 for Canada, leaving his cellphone behind; his wife remained and was threatened by ABT calls, then left for Canada in XXXX 2018.
propositions.quote: He left Bangladesh in XXXX 2018 and came to Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. He left his cell phone in Bangladesh. His wife remained in Bangladesh. The ABT kept calling on the cellphone and threatened her. She left Bangladesh in XXXX of 2018 and came to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Appellant received threats while with his mother and friend, left Bangladesh for Canada leaving his phone; his wife was threatened then also came to Canada.

propositions.text: In XXXX 2018, the Principal Appellant's brother died; ABT threatened another brother to join and pay or face harm, threatening to kill the Principal Appellant and his wife if he returned.
propositions.quote: In XXXX 2018, the Principal Appellant's brother died. The ABT told the Principal Appellant's other brother that they XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX to the deceased brother. They would do the same to him unless he joined the ABT and paid them money. They told him that, if the Principal Appellant returned, they would kill the Principal Appellant and his wife, the Associate Appellant.

paragraphs.summary: In XXXX 2018, ABT threatened the Principal Appellant's family to join or pay, threatening to kill the Principal Appellant and his wife if he returned.

propositions.text: The RPD found state protection was available and an internal flight alternative in Chittagong; the Appellants appealed to RAD without new evidence or hearing request.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that state protection was available for the Appellants. Further, it found that the Appellants had an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Chittagong. The Appellants have appealed to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD). They have not submitted any new evidence nor have they requested a hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found state protection and an internal flight alternative in Chittagong; the Appellants appealed without new evidence or hearing request.

propositions.text: The RAD conducted an independent assessment including listening to the full RPD hearing recording, which is in evidence.
propositions.quote: I have conducted an independent assessment of the evidence and arguments. This review includes listening to the entire recording of the RPD hearing. This recording is in evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD conducted an independent assessment including listening to the full RPD hearing recording, which is in evidence.

propositions.text: The RAD considered the most recent National Documentation Package (NDP) and gave notice to the Appellant to respond, but received no response.
propositions.quote: In addition to the National Documentation Package (NDP) that was on record with the RPD and in keeping with the "Policy on National Documentation Packages in Refugee Determination Proceedings",1 the RAD has also considered the most recent NDP at the time of writing the decision. On May 26, 2020, the RAD provided notice to the Appellant that it would be doing so, in particular, item 7.9 of the NDP from March 31, 2020. The Appellant was given two weeks to provide a response. As of the date of this decision, there has not been any response from Counsel.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD considered the most recent NDP and gave notice to the Appellant to respond, but received no response.

propositions.text: The issue is whether the Appellants are persons in need of protection under section 97 of the Act, given no nexus to a Convention refugee ground.
propositions.quote: The Appellants do not challenge the RPD's finding that there was not a nexus to a ground under the definition of a Convention refugee in accordance with section 96 of the Act. Having reviewed the evidence, I have come to the same conclusion; I see no need to intervene to prevent an injustice.2 The issue is whether the Appellants are persons in need of protection in accordance with section 97 of the Act. In other words, is there a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Bangladesh? Is there State Protection in Bangladesh?

paragraphs.summary: The issue is whether the Appellants are persons in need of protection under section 97 of the Act, given no nexus to a Convention refugee ground.

propositions.text: The RPD found state protection is available in Bangladesh.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that there was state protection in Bangladesh.

propositions.text: The Appellants argue police are corrupt and state protection is not available.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the police are corrupt, and it is not available.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found state protection is available; the Appellants argue police corruption means protection is unavailable.

propositions.text: Evidence about state protection is mixed: police corruption is undisputed, but there is evidence of state commitment to eradicate ABT with decreased attacks and increased arrests.
propositions.quote: The evidence about state protection is mixed. It is not disputed that the police are corrupt. However, there is also objective and neutral evidence of state commitment to eradicate the ABT. In particular, terrorist attacks have decreased, and arrests against ABT members have increased.3 Other evidence states that attacks are increasing but confirms that the ABT is banned and that there is zero tolerance of terrorism in Bangladesh.4 Further, the state apparatus to enforce the law has significant flaws and is feeble.5

paragraphs.summary: Evidence about state protection is mixed: police corruption is undisputed, but there is evidence of state commitment to eradicate ABT with decreased attacks and increased arrests.

propositions.text: There is not consistent state protection, but the issue is the degree of risk from ABT throughout Bangladesh, not a risk everywhere.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Appellants that there is not consistent state protection. However, the issue is the degree of risk from the ABT throughout Bangladesh. In other words, there is not a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment throughout Bangladesh.

paragraphs.summary: There is not consistent state protection, but the issue is the degree of risk from ABT throughout Bangladesh, not a risk everywhere.

propositions.text: If the Appellants have an internal flight alternative, they are not persons in need of protection; the RPD found an IFA in Chittagong.
propositions.quote: If the Appellants have an internal flight alternative, they are not persons in need of protection. In this case, the RPD found that there was an IFA in Chittagong.

paragraphs.summary: If the Appellants have an internal flight alternative, they are not persons in need of protection; the RPD found an IFA in Chittagong.

propositions.text: The test for IFA is two-pronged from Rasaratnam: no serious risk in the area and it is reasonable to seek refuge there.
propositions.quote: The test for assessing an IFA is two-pronged and is set out in the Federal Court of Appeal's decision in Rasaratnam.6 (1) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. (2) Moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for him to seek refuge there.7

paragraphs.summary: The test for IFA is two-pronged from Rasaratnam: no serious risk in the area and it is reasonable to seek refuge there.

propositions.text: Both prongs must be satisfied; burden is on appellant to disprove IFA; IFA must be realistic and not cause undue hardship.
propositions.quote: Both prongs must be satisfied to find that an appellant has an IFA. Once the issue of IFA has been raised and the potential IFAs have been identified, the burden of proof rests with an appellant to show that he/she does not have an IFA. The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of the region for that purpose taking into account an appellant's personal circumstances. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. An appellant cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or undergo undue hardship in traveling there and staying there.

paragraphs.summary: Both prongs must be satisfied; burden is on appellant to disprove IFA; IFA must be realistic and not cause undue hardship.

propositions.text: Objective evidence supports that the Appellants can relocate; UK Home Office notes non-state actor pursued appellants can relocate in Bangladesh; IFA is Chittagong.
propositions.quote: In general, the objective evidence supports a conclusion that the Appellants can relocate. The UK Home Office notes that appellants who are pursued by non-state actors are able to relocate in Bangladesh.8 However, the individual circumstances of the Appellants should be considered. In this case, the IFA identified was Chittagong.

paragraphs.summary: Objective evidence supports that the Appellants can relocate; UK Home Office notes non-state actor pursued appellants can relocate in Bangladesh; IFA is Chittagong.

propositions.text: The Appellants argue ABT has connections with JMB and ISIS, making them findable in Chittagong.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the ABT have connections with the Jamaatul Mujahideen Bangladesh (JMB) and, consequently, with ISIS.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows fluid militant groups; ABT renamed Ansar-ul-Islam; ABT aims to make Bangladesh Islamic state; some sources say ABT joined violent JMB splinter; others say ABT worked with JMB; evidence supports ABT-ISIS link.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence regarding the militants in Bangladesh reflect the fluid and changing nature of the militant groups. The ABT is said to have changed its name to Ansar-ul-Islam.9 There is documentary evidence that the ABT has a singular goal of making Bangladesh an Islamic state. Some sources state that it joined forces with a violent splinter of the JMB to be part of a "neo JMB".10 Other sources state that the ABT has worked with JMB. Further, the documentary evidence does support a link between the ABT and ISIS.11

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue ABT has connections with JMB and ISIS, making them findable in Chittagong; evidence shows fluid militant groups and ABT-ISIS links.

propositions.text: Evidence about ISIS presence in Bangladesh is unclear; no terrorism reports in 2018.
propositions.quote: The evidence about the level of ISIS's presence in Bangladesh is unclear. While there is ISIS in Bangladesh, there were no reports of terrorism in 2018.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence of ABT presence in Chittagong posing risk to Appellants.
propositions.quote: the Appellants have not provided sufficient evidence to show that there is a presence of ABT that would present a risk to them in Chittagong.

propositions.text: Appellants targeted for business in Dhaka; no evidence that business exists in Chittagong.
propositions.quote: The Appellants were targeted for their business in Dhaka; there is insufficient evidence that this business, that attracted the militants, is present in Chittagong.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant closed his company, removing reason for risk in Chittagong.
propositions.quote: according to the Principal Appellant's narrative in his Basis of Claim (BOC), he has closed his company.

propositions.text: Lack of business that drew militants weighs against likelihood of persecution in Chittagong.
propositions.quote: the lack of the business that drew their attention is a factor that weighs against the likelihood of persecution in Chittagong.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds unclear ISIS presence, insufficient ABT risk evidence in Chittagong; business closed, reducing persecution likelihood.

propositions.text: State has responded to ABT; ABT less active now.
propositions.quote: it appears that the state has launched a response to the ABT, and they are less active.

propositions.text: State response insufficient to prove protection but supports finding of low risk to Appellants.
propositions.quote: While this may not be sufficient evidence to find that there is state protection, it is sufficient evidence to weigh in favour of a finding that there is not a likelihood of risk to the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds state response reduced ABT activity, supporting low risk to Appellants though not proving protection.

propositions.text: Appellants argue they can be easily found via cell phone GPS without expertise.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that they could be easily found through their cell phone. They state that it does not require a lot of expertise on GPS and cell phones to do so. It is easily done, and anyone can do it.

propositions.text: Appellants do not explain how tracking is done or provide supporting evidence.
propositions.quote: they do not explain how it is done, or how anyone can do it. They do not show which evidence supports their claim that anyone can track a person through their cell phones.

propositions.text: Principal and Associate Appellants had same cell phone near Dhaka without agents knowing their location.
propositions.quote: the Principal Appellant and the Associate Appellant had the same cell phone for a significant amount of time while they were close to Dhaka, and there is insufficient evidence to find that the agents of persecution knew where they were.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant had cell phone until XXXX 2018, was in Dhaka, no harm despite calls and one visit to mother.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant had the cell phone until XXXX 2018 when he left; he was even in Dhaka with it. They called him, and while his mother said they came to her house one time, there was not another confrontation with the Principal Appellant even when he returned to Dhaka and lived there for months.

propositions.text: Associate Appellant was called by ABT but not tracked or found while in Bangladesh until XXXX 2018.
propositions.quote: When the Associate Appellant left Dhaka, the ABT called her. However, she was in Bangladesh until XXXX 2018, and they did not track her down or find her.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue easy cell phone tracking; court finds no explanation or evidence and notes no harm despite phone use near Dhaka.

propositions.text: Associate Appellant likely had same cell phone as Principal Appellant; no testimony to contrary.
propositions.quote: the Associate Appellant likely had the same cell phone that the Principal Appellant had. The Associate Appellant did not testify that it was a different cell phone, and the Principal Appellant testified that he left his cell phone in Bangladesh.

propositions.text: Agents did not find or harm Appellants when sharing cell phone near Dhaka; less likely in remote Chittagong.
propositions.quote: As the agents of persecution did not find and harm the Appellants when they had the same cell phone in and around Dhaka, the likelihood that the cellphone would lead the agents of persecution to the Appellants is even less in Chittagong.

propositions.text: Geographic remoteness of Chittagong reduces likelihood of agents finding Appellants via cell phone.
propositions.quote: the geographic remoteness of Chittagong from the agents of persecution is a factor in assessing the cell phone and the agent of persecution's likelihood in finding the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Associate Appellant likely shared cell phone; no harm near Dhaka; remoteness of Chittagong reduces risk.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant argues he received threats after closing company.
propositions.quote: While the Principal Appellant argues that he still received threats after closing the company,

propositions.text: Threats received on same cell phone while near Dhaka; no company now reduces likelihood ABT would find him.
propositions.quote: he received the threats on the same cell phone, and he was still within the vicinity of Dhaka. It was still close to the time of the first threats. The fact that he does not still have the company is a factor that weighs against a finding that the ABT would likely find him.

paragraphs.summary: Appellant claims post-closure threats; court finds threats near Dhaka on same phone and no company reduces ABT risk.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant did not think to discard cell phone despite ongoing ABT calls to him and wife.
propositions.quote: the Principal Appellant points out that he testified that he did not think of getting rid of the cell phone even after the ABT kept calling him, he and his wife, the Associate Appellant, claim that she received calls after he left Bangladesh.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant's explanation does not clarify why they did not discard phone despite ongoing issue.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant's explanation of not thinking about it does not explain why they did not do so when it was an ongoing issue.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants say phone not discarded despite calls; court finds explanation insufficient for ongoing issue.

propositions.text: Appellants argue threats continued as late as October 2018.
propositions.quote: While the Appellants argue that there were threats as late as when his brother received a threat against them in October 2018,

propositions.text: Passage of over 1.5 years reduces likelihood ABT can find Appellants.
propositions.quote: that was over one and a half years ago. With the passage of time, the likelihood that the ABT would be able to find the Appellants is even more remote.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants cite October 2018 threats; court finds time passage reduces ABT's ability to find them.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant stayed in Dhaka after incident, rented house, agents came to house.
propositions.quote: the Principal Appellant testified that he stayed in Dhaka for a few days after the incident in XXXX and rented a house before going to his mother's home. The agents of persecution came to his house.

propositions.text: RPD questioned omission of this incident from BOC.
propositions.quote: The RPD questioned why this incident was not in the BOC,

propositions.text: Principal Appellant said he summarized incident, so did not mention it in BOC.
propositions.quote: the Principal Appellant responded that he was trying to summarize the incident, so he did not mention it.

propositions.text: Court finds explanation unreasonable; omission of material incident weighs against credibility.
propositions.quote: I do not find that this explanation is reasonable. The BOC is quite detailed, and the Appellant did amend it prior to the hearing. Incidents of the agents of persecution seeking the Principal Appellant are important and material; that this incident was not included in the BOC weighs against its credibility.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Principal Appellant's omission of house incident from BOC unreasonable, undermining credibility.

propositions.text: Appellants argue ABT found and killed Principal Appellant's brother, so could find Appellants.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the ABT found the Principal Appellant's brother and killed him, so they could find the Appellants as well.

propositions.text: Is there sufficient evidence that ABT found and killed Principal Appellant's brother?
propositions.quote: Is there sufficient evidence that the ABT found and killed the Principal Appellant's brother?

propositions.text: Two death certificates exist: one hospital document in English without heading, one government Bengali document.
propositions.quote: There are two death certificates. One appears to be from a hospital, although there is no heading on the document. A doctor and a resident have signed it. There is a translation on record. The original document has headings in the Bengali language but is completed in English. ... The other document is a government document. The original is completed in the Bengali language.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants claim ABT killed brother; court questions sufficiency of evidence and notes two death certificates.

propositions.text: Hospital death certificate not credible due to English language use and lack of heading.
propositions.quote: I find that the death certificate signed by the doctor is not a credible document. Bengali is the official language of Bangladesh, and at least 98% of people use it. It is unclear why the hospital would complete the document in the English language that less than two percent of the population use. It is also unclear why the document would not have a heading.

propositions.text: Vague comment on cause of death not compelling evidence of ABT involvement.
propositions.quote: I do not find that the comment "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX" is compelling evidence that the brother was XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX from the ABT; it is too vague.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds hospital death certificate not credible and cause of death comment too vague to prove ABT involvement.

propositions.text: Appellants argue hospital need not state cause of death.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the hospital does not have to state the cause of the XXXX.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence of barrier to obtaining medical report confirming cause of death.
propositions.quote: there is insufficient evidence of any barrier to acquiring a medical report which, if they hospital told the brother the deceased brother was XXXX, could confirm information that the hospital had already shared this information and why they could not ascertain the XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

propositions.text: Flawed evidence weakens finding that brother was XXXX or ABT killed him.
propositions.quote: Given the flaws with the evidence that the Principal Appellant's brother was XXXX, it would have assisted a finding that it is more likely than not that the deceased brother was XXXX. Similarly, there is not a statement from the Principal Appellant's other brother indicating that he talked to the ABT. Sufficient evidence that the deceased brother was XXXX is necessary before continuing to the second finding that it is more likely than not that the ABT XXXX the deceased brother.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue hospital need not state cause; court finds insufficient evidence and flawed proof of brother's death by ABT.

propositions.text: Government death certificate in Bengali with letterhead more credible but does not mention XXXX or ABT involvement.
propositions.quote: The other death certificate is a more credible document. It is in the Bengali language. It has a letterhead. For cause of death, it has "XXXX XXXX XXXX" written. It does not mention XXXX.

propositions.text: Document does not support finding deceased brother was XXXX.
propositions.quote: the document does not support a finding that the deceased brother was XXXX.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds government death certificate more credible but does not support brother's death by ABT.

propositions.text: Brother reported hospital told him deceased was XXXX; General Diary is hearsay and lacks corroboration.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant's brother reported to the police that the hospital told him that the other brother was XXXX. The General Diary excerpt given to the police most closely resembles a letter to the police from the Principal Appellant's brother. ... It simply states that the Principal Appellant's brother laid a complaint. ... The brother is reporting what the hospital told him. Hearsay evidence is admissible evidence, but it is inherently not as reliable and/or accurate as direct evidence.

propositions.text: No medical report or corroborative evidence supports brother was XXXX or ABT killed him.
propositions.quote: The Appellants did provide a death certificate that they claim is from the hospital, they have not provided a medical report from it. The issues with the hospital's death certificate have been noted. The Appellants have not provided sufficient corroborative evidence that supports a conclusion that it is more likely than not that the Principal Appellant's brother was XXXX. Further, the likelihood that it was the ABT who XXXX him is even more remote.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds brother's report hearsay, no corroboration or medical report supports ABT killing brother.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence that brother died due to ABT; evidence too flawed to find event likely occurred.
propositions.quote: I find that there is insufficient evidence that the Principal Appellant's brother died because he was XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The evidence supporting this allegation is too flawed to be given weight that leads to a likelihood that the event occurred. The Appellants have not established it is more likely than not that this occurred.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes insufficient evidence brother died due to ABT; evidence too flawed to find event likely.

propositions.text: Likelihood Appellants need protection in Chittagong undermined by inconsistent evidence.
propositions.quote: I find that the likelihood that the Appellants are in need of protection in Chittagong is undermined by the inconsistency in the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds inconsistent evidence undermines Appellants' need for protection in Chittagong.

propositions.text: Appellants request RAD substitute RPD decision finding them persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: In the Appellant's Memorandum, the Appellants have requested that I substitute the RPD's decision for one that the Appellants are persons in need of protection.

propositions.text: Issues with evidence consistency considered independently by court; no need to put to Appellants for submissions as evidence is on record.
propositions.quote: As part of my independent review of the evidence, I have considered these inconsistencies. As stated by the Federal Court, in so doing, I do not find that, in this case, I have to put them to the Appellants to provide an opportunity to provide submissions, as the evidence is already on record.

propositions.text: RPD has no duty to confront claimants with concerns about their own documents; same applies to RAD.
propositions.quote: Further, as the RPD does not have a duty to confront claimants with concerns regarding their own documents, the same reasoning should apply to the RAD.

propositions.text: No obligation to confront Appellants with discrepancies as evidence is not extrinsic.
propositions.quote: Given that it is not extrinsic evidence, there is no obligation to confront the Appellants with discrepancies in the evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants seek substitution; court independently reviews evidence inconsistencies, no obligation to confront Appellants.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant testified of ABT visits with inconsistent numbers of people compared to police report.
propositions.quote: the Principal Appellant testified that, on one occasion, there were five people from the ABT who came to his office, and in XXXX 2018, the same five people came with three more people. The police report for the incident in XXXX 2018 only states that there were five ABT members.

propositions.text: Inconsistency on central narrative point noted but given little weight as Principal Appellant not given chance to address it.
propositions.quote: This is inconsistent regarding a central point of the narrative. However, I do not give these considerations significant weight, as the Principal Appellant was not given the opportunity to address it.

paragraphs.summary: Court notes inconsistency in ABT visit numbers but gives little weight as Principal Appellant not given chance to explain.

propositions.text: Police crime diary excerpts confirm complaints made but lack police verification or investigation.
propositions.quote: the excerpts from the police crime diaries record complaints that are made by the Principal Appellant and his brother. They confirm that complaints were made, but they do not confirm that the police verified the accounts or performed any form of investigation to support the accounts therein.

propositions.text: Police excerpts have limited probative value; insufficient to find events likely occurred.
propositions.quote: These excerpts have limited probative value. They do not provide sufficient evidence to find that it is more likely than not that the events described actually occurred.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds police diary excerpts confirm complaints but lack verification, thus limited probative value.

propositions.text: Letters from Principal Appellant's mother and councillor provided; councillor's letter inconsistent with Appellants' account and has translation issues.
propositions.quote: the Appellants have provided letters from the Principal Appellant's mother and a "councilor" [sic]. These letters have notarial stamps that state that they are authenticated. The councillor certifies that the Principal Appellant was attacked by the ABT several times. The letter does not appear to be consistent with the Appellants' account of events. The grammar in this letter is difficult, and there may be issues with translation; but while the Principal Appellant testified that he was threatened, he did not state that he was attacked by the ABT on several occasions.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds letters from mother and councillor; councillor's letter inconsistent and has translation issues.

propositions.text: Mother's letter authenticated but likely typed; vague about ABT visits and inconsistent with BOC.
propositions.quote: The letter of the Principal Appellant's mother states that the Principal Appellant stayed with her from XXXX XXXX to XXXX and that members of the ABT went to her home to find the Principal Appellant. ... There is insufficient evidence that the mother actually wrote the letter, it appears typed. ... the account of the ABT going to her home is vague. ... she provides a minimal description. Further, the account of the ABT going to his mother's house is inconsistent with the BOC that does not mention this event.

propositions.text: RPD questioned discrepancy about ABT visit to mother's home.
propositions.quote: The RPD questioned the Appellant about this discrepancy.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant said he did not include event in BOC because he learned of it after returning to Dhaka but before completing BOC.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant stated that he did not include it in the BOC because he found out about it after he went back to Dhaka, but that was before he completed his BOC.

propositions.text: Court finds explanation unreasonable; inconsistency weighs against credibility of ABT visit to mother's home.
propositions.quote: I do not find that this explanation is reasonable; this inconsistency weighs against the credibility of the likelihood that the agents of persecution went to his home.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds mother's letter vague and inconsistent with BOC; explanation unreasonable, undermining credibility of ABT visit claim.

propositions.text: Notary seal authenticates signatures but letters are not affidavits and lack sworn truthfulness
propositions.quote: The purpose of the notary seal appears to be to authenticate that the mother and the councillor signed the letters. However, they are not affidavits. The signatories have not sworn or affirmed that the information is true.

propositions.text: Seal and stamps alone do not justify giving letters more weight
propositions.quote: I do not find that the presence of a seal and stamps are sufficient to provide reason to give the letters more weight.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the notary seal authenticates signatures but letters are not affidavits and seals alone don't justify more weight.

propositions.text: Appellants' self-written letters only repeat their narrative
propositions.quote: Further, while the Appellants provided letters that they wrote themselves to support their claims, I find that these letters only reiterate their narrative.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the appellants' self-written letters merely reiterate their narrative.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence that appellants face risk to life or cruel treatment in Chittagong
propositions.quote: I find that there is insufficient evidence that it is more likely than not that the Appellants face a risk to their lives or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Chittagong.

propositions.text: Is it reasonable for the Appellants to relocate in Bangladesh?
propositions.quote: Is it reasonable for the Appellants to relocate in Bangladesh?

paragraphs.summary: The court finds insufficient evidence of risk to appellants in Chittagong and raises the issue of reasonableness of relocation.

propositions.text: Record on relocation issue is limited but appellants had two opportunities to provide evidence
propositions.quote: The record on this issue is limited. However, the Appellants have had an opportunity to provide evidence for Chittagong on two occasions-both at the RPD and at the RAD.

propositions.text: Best available evidence is relied on and is sufficient for a confident decision
propositions.quote: For this appeal. I am relying on the best evidence available. I have reviewed and considered the record. I find that it is sufficient to make a sound decision with confidence on this issue.

propositions.text: Reasons are not speculative due to lack of evidence
propositions.quote: In other words, I do not find that there is such a paucity of evidence in this case that the reasons are speculative.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the record limited but sufficient and not speculative to decide on relocation reasonableness.

propositions.text: Appellants have burden of proof and knew relocation was an issue
propositions.quote: It is worth noting that the Appellants have the burden of proof. The Appellants were aware that this was an issue and raised the issue of an IFA in their memorandum.

propositions.text: Appellants had opportunity to submit new evidence but did not
propositions.quote: Although they had the opportunity to request to submit new evidence, they did not do so.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence that relocation is unreasonable
propositions.quote: The Appellants have provided insufficient evidence that it is unreasonable for them to relocate.

propositions.text: Record supports finding that relocation is not unreasonable
propositions.quote: Further, the record, in its totality, supports a finding that there is insufficient evidence to conclude that it is unreasonable for the Appellants to relocate.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellants had burden and opportunity but provided insufficient evidence that relocation is unreasonable.

propositions.text: High threshold to show IFA unreasonable requires proof of life or safety jeopardy in Chittagong
propositions.quote: I am mindful of the high threshold that is required to show that an IFA is unreasonable; the Federal Court of Appeal has held that there must be proof of adverse conditions that would jeopardize the life and safety of the Appellants when travelling or living in Chittagong.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the high legal threshold to prove an IFA is unreasonable requires proof of jeopardy to life or safety.

propositions.text: Appellants are Bengali, Muslim, and speak Bengali, the predominant ethnic group, faith, and language in Bangladesh
propositions.quote: As noted by the RPD, the Appellants are Bengali, which is the predominant ethnic group in Bangladesh. They are Muslim, which is the predominant faith in Bangladesh. Further, they speak Bengali, which is the language of Bangladesh.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence of ethnic, religious or language barriers for appellants
propositions.quote: There is insufficient evidence of any ethnic, religious or language barrier for the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found appellants share predominant ethnicity, religion, and language; the court finds no evidence of barriers.

propositions.text: Appellants have significant resources and education, including a BA and business experience
propositions.quote: The Appellants have significant resources. The Principal Appellant is well educated and has a BA in XXXX and XXXX XXXX. He has significant work experience. He owned and ran a XXXX XXXX XXXX company for 10 years.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence of business problems except ABT attention
propositions.quote: There is insufficient evidence to conclude that it is more likely than not that there were problems with the business, other than attracting the attention of the ABT.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence of financial problems
propositions.quote: There is insufficient evidence that the Appellants had any financial problems.

propositions.text: Bangladesh economy has grown about 6% annually and reached lower-middle income status in 2014
propositions.quote: I note that the economy in Bangladesh has grown about 6% on average annually for the last two decades and, in 2014, reached the World Bank lower-middle income status.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellants have resources, education, business experience, no financial problems, and notes Bangladesh's economic growth.

propositions.text: Associate Appellant described as housewife but testified to working in family company
propositions.quote: Further, while the Associate Appellant wrote in the Canadian government's Citizenship and Immigration Canada, Schedule A that she was a housewife, she testified that she went into the company and worked in it when he was not there and was travelling.

propositions.text: Associate Appellant has some business experience
propositions.quote: She has some business experience.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the associate appellant has some business experience despite describing herself as a housewife.

propositions.text: Work experience is a skill for appellants
propositions.quote: The work experience is a skill for the Appellants.

propositions.text: No evidence of barriers to employment, housing, medical care or other factors affecting IFA reasonableness
propositions.quote: They have not provided evidence that there is any barrier to finding employment in Chittagong. I have noted evidence of economic growth in Bangladesh. Further, they have not provided evidence of issues with housing, medical care, or any of the factors that would apply to them in an analysis of whether an IFA is reasonable; nor did I see any in my review of the evidence on record.

propositions.text: Overall insufficient evidence of barriers
propositions.quote: Overall, there is insufficient evidence of barriers.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds appellants' work experience is a skill and there is insufficient evidence of barriers to employment or living in Chittagong.

propositions.text: Appellants claim lack of friends and family support in Chittagong
propositions.quote: The Appellants have pointed out that they have a lack of friends and family in Chittagong; they do not have support.

propositions.text: Court considers lack of support but weighs it against appellants' significant resources
propositions.quote: I have considered this factor. I find that, in this case, it must be weighed in the context of Appellants who have significant resources.

propositions.text: Appellants had opportunity to provide more evidence but did not
propositions.quote: Further, despite being given the opportunity to provide evidence and specifically asked if they had anything else to add to this issue at the hearing, they have not provided sufficient evidence of barriers that they would have to face.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants argue lack of support; court weighs this against their resources and finds insufficient evidence of barriers.

propositions.text: No sufficient evidence of barriers to show relocation to Chittagong is unreasonable
propositions.quote: Having considered the record, I do not find that there is sufficient evidence of barriers to these Appellants in their circumstances to show that it would be unreasonable for them to relocate and live in Chittagong.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds insufficient evidence of barriers making relocation to Chittagong unreasonable.

propositions.text: Appeal dismissed; RPD decision confirmed that appellants are not refugees or persons in need of protection
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that appellants are not refugees or in need of protection.
